slides.title: Reading the report
slides.sub: Tracebacks, raised errors, and notes
slides.notes:
SAY: Error signalling is the way a program says that something has gone wrong. In Python the saying is done with exceptions: an exception is an object that carries a description of the problem and travels up through the running code until something handles it.

slides.title: The bug you can visit in a museum

items.cap: the Mark II logbook page, moth taped in - U.S. Navy photo, public domain

items: 9 September 1947: the Mark II stops
Relay 70, panel F: a moth
'First actual case of bug being found'
The page survives at the Smithsonian

items.who: Grace Hopper's Harvard Mark II team
items.where: the machine's logbook - now at the Smithsonian

slides.notes:
STORY (1947-09-09): On 9 September 1947 the Harvard Mark II stopped, and the operators traced the fault to a moth caught in relay 70 of panel F. They taped the insect into the logbook with the note 'First actual case of bug being found' - the joke being that engineers already said 'bug' for faults. The page, moth and all, survives at the Smithsonian, and the photograph on this slide is the Navy's own. Debugging has meant removing the moth ever since.
SOURCE: The Mark II logbook page of 1947-09-09, 'First actual case of bug being found', held by the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History; photograph courtesy of the Naval Surface Warfare Center, Dahlgren (public domain). Note: a common file title misdates it 1945; the log page itself is dated September 9, 1947.
slides.take: Every bug since has been a metaphor; this one had wings

slides.title: Assertions
slides.sub: Executable assumptions
slides.notes:
SAY: An assertion is a statement that a certain condition must be true at a certain point of a program, together with a check that stops the program at once if it is not. The chapter calls an assertion a sanity check, a test that makes sure the code is not doing something obviously wrong, and it performs such checks with the assert statement, which raises an AssertionError exception when the check fails (Sweigart, 2025).
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 5 - Assertion.

slides.title: Logging
slides.sub: The print statement that grew up
slides.notes:
SAY: Logging is the practice of making a program write down what it does while it runs. The Python logging HOWTO defines it as a means of tracking events that happen when some software runs: the developer adds logging calls to the code to indicate that certain events have occurred, and each event is described by a message and has an importance, which is called its level or severity (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
FULL TEXT: course page, chapter 5 - Logging.

slides.title: The most effective debugging tool

items.cap: Brian Kernighan at Bell Labs - photo: Ben Lowe, CC BY 2.0

items: Bell Labs, 1979: 'careful thought, coupled with
judiciously placed print statements'
This chapter agrees - then gives print levels,
timestamps, files, and an off switch

items.where: 'Unix for Beginners', the Bell Labs memorandum

slides.notes:
STORY (1979): In a 1979 Bell Labs paper Kernighan wrote the sentence every debugger vendor has to argue with: 'The most effective debugging tool is still careful thought, coupled with judiciously placed print statements.' This chapter agrees, then upgrades the print statement into logging. Same idea - but with levels, timestamps, files, and an off switch that does not require deleting your evidence.
SOURCE: Brian W. Kernighan, 'Unix for Beginners' (Bell Laboratories, 1979), the 'careful thought... judiciously placed print statements' sentence; biography and bibliography at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Kernighan. Photo: Ben Lowe, CC BY 2.0, at Bell Labs.
slides.take: Logging is the print statement that grew up

slides.title: A logging system with a birth certificate
slides.sub: PEP 282, 2002; stdlib since Python 2.3

items: PEP 282 (2002), Vinay Sajip and Trent Mick - modelled on log4j's levels
In the standard library since Python 2.3; these slides run that exact machinery

items.who: Vinay Sajip and Trent Mick, through the PEP process
items.where: peps.python.org - and the logging module these slides run

slides.notes:
STORY (PEP 282, 2002; stdlib since Python 2.3): Python's logging module did not drift into the language; it was proposed as PEP 282 in 2002 by Vinay Sajip and Trent Mick, modelled on log4j's levels, and entered the standard library in Python 2.3. DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL - the five-step ladder on these slides is that PEP's design, and the chapter's demos run it: to the console, to a file, forced, and disabled.
SOURCE: PEP 282, 'A Logging System', authors Vinay Sajip and Trent Mick (2002), implemented as the standard library's logging module from Python 2.3 (peps.python.org/pep-0282).
slides.take: The five log levels are a 2002 design decision

slides.sub: breakpoint() - a conversation mid-thought

items: breakpoint() drops you into pdb at that line
n steps over; s steps in; p prints a name
c continues; q quits the session
The lab: watch total grow, step by step
n next
s step in
p name
c continue
q quit

slides.notes:
SAY: The debugger is a tool that runs a program one instruction at a time and lets the programmer look at the program between the steps. The chapter defines it as a feature of the Mu editor that executes a program one instruction at a time, giving a chance to inspect the values in variables while the code runs and to track how the values change over the course of the program (Sweigart, 2025).
